questions.problem:
The second-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}-10y=0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}+10y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}+10{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=10{x}_{1}+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=10{x}_{1}+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}.$

questions.problem:
The third-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{‴}-6\sqrt{t}\,{y}^{″}+12{y}^{′}=0,\,y(1)=-2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2,\,{y}^{″}(1)=-3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=q \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{3}(1)=r\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t),$ and $p,$ $q$ and $r$ are constants. Calculate  $(p+q-r)\cdot f(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={x}_{1}(1)=-2 \\ {y}^{′}(1) & ={x}_{2}(1)=2 \\ {y}^{″}(1) & ={x}_{3}(1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=6\sqrt{t}\,{y}^{″}-12{y}^{′}.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}-12{x}_{2}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=-2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=2 \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=-12{x}_{2}+6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3},\, & {x}_{3}(1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=-2,q=2,r=-3,f(t)=-12{x}_{2}+6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p+q-r)\cdot f(t) & =(-2+2-(-3))(-12{x}_{2}+6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}) \\  & =(-2+2+3)(-12{x}_{2}+6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}) \\  & =3(-6)(2{x}_{2}-\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}) \\  & =-18(2{x}_{2}-\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-ty=0,\,y(2)=-2,\,{y}^{′}(2)=-3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(2)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(2)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & ={x}_{1}(2)=-2 \\ {y}^{′}(2) & ={x}_{2}(2)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-4{y}^{′}+ty.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-4{x}_{2}+t{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(2)=-2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=t{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(2)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=-2,q=-3,f(t)=t{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(-2-(-3))(t{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}) \\  & =(1)(t{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}) \\  & =t{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
The second-order differential equation $3{y}^{″}+9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}+y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

$$
{y}^{″}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}-\frac{1}{3}y.
$$

$$
{y}^{″}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{1}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

$$
{y}^{″}=4{y}^{′}-3y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{1}.
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous ODE to a First-Order System
canonical_examples.problem:
The third-order differential equation 

$$
y''' - 3\sqrt{t}\, y'' + t^3 y' - 4t^2 y= 0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t)$ and $x_3(t) = y''(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1, x_2,$ and $x_3.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y'''),$ we obtain

$$
y''' = 3\sqrt{t}\,y'' - t^3 y' + 4t^2 y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
y''' = 3\sqrt{t}\, x_3 - t^3 x_2 + 4t^2 x_1.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=4{t}^{2}\,{x}_{1}-{t}^{3}{x}_{2}+3\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t) = 4t^2 x_1 - t^3 x_2 + 3\sqrt{t} \,x_3.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem to a First-Order System
canonical_examples.problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
y''  + y' - 6y= 0 , \quad y(0)= 1, \quad y'(0)= 4
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(0)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={x}_{1}(0)=1 \\ {y}^{′}(0) & ={x}_{2}(0)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y''),$ we obtain

$$
y'' = - y' + 6y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
y'' = - x_2 + 6x_1.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=1 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=6{x}_{1}-{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=1, q=4, f(t) = 6x_1 - x_2,$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(1-4)(6{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}) \\  & =-3(6{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}).\end{aligned}
$$
